d: A doer of that which is good.

e.t: This word means “doing good” and can describe “one who does good.” It points to good action, whether emphasizing the action itself or the person carrying it out. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Peter 2:14. The word’s basic sense is clear, while the precise role it plays in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

d: A brother, member of the same religious community, especially a fellow-Christian.

e.t: This word means “brother” and, in its plural form, “brothers.” It names a male sibling and is commonly used to address or describe more than one brother. The word appears 343 times in the Greek New Testament, so it is a well-established term used throughout that corpus. Its exact reference—whether to a particular family member or a group addressed as brothers—depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

d: To take captive (in war); to subdue, ensnare.
me: Verb, Future, Passive, Indicative, third, Plural

Verb, Present, Active, Participle, Nominative, Plural, Masculine

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “capturing,” “to capture,” or “to take captive.” It describes taking someone captive or bringing a person under another’s control. The word appears four times in the Greek New Testament, each time in a different verse. Its uses include both literal captivity and the broader idea of being seized or brought into submission, but the precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage. It is a verb, so it expresses an action rather than naming a person, place, or thing.

d: Hearing, faculty of hearing, ear; report, rumor.

e.t: This word means “hearing,” referring to receiving or perceiving what is spoken or otherwise communicated. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 24 times across 22 verses, so it can describe the act of hearing or the report that reaches someone. Its basic sense remains focused on hearing rather than on a particular response or interpretation. The surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis is on hearing itself or on what has been heard.

d: Profitless, unprofitable, ruinous, detrimental.

e.t: This word describes something that is unprofitable or disadvantageous—something that does not provide a useful gain or benefit. It functions as a descriptive word, pointing to the lack of advantage in whatever it qualifies. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Hebrews 13:17. The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense is clear: something brings no profit or advantage rather than producing a beneficial result.

d: To wash dirt off.
me: Verb, Aorist, Middle, Indicative, third, Singular

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to wash off.” It describes the act of removing something by washing, functioning as a verb rather than naming an object or person. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in Matthew 27:24. Its basic sense is straightforward: something is washed away or removed through washing. The precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself centers on washing something off or away.

d: To fit, join; (the middle indicating deep personal interest) to espouse, betroth; to take a wife, give in marriage.
me: Verb, Aorist, Middle, Indicative, first, Singular

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to betroth” or “to promise for marriage.” It describes committing someone to a future marriage, pointing to a marriage promise rather than marriage itself. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in 2 Corinthians 11:2. Since the verse text and surrounding context are not included here, this entry states the word’s ordinary meaning; the passage determines how that promise functions in its sentence.

d: Tomorrow.
me: ADVerb or adverb and particle combined

e.t: This word means “tomorrow,” referring to the day after today. It can point to a future day in ordinary planning, expected events, or teaching about how people should view the future. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 14 times, including passages that speak about tomorrow as something people may anticipate but cannot fully control. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic reference remains the coming day.

d: A missile, dart, javelin, arrow.

e.t: This word means “arrow” or “arrows,” referring to a projectile shot through the air. It is a concrete noun that names the object itself, not the act of shooting or the person who uses it. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Ephesians 6:16. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text and context, but its ordinary meaning remains the same: an arrow, or arrows considered as a group. The word therefore provides a straightforward picture of a weapon used against a target.

d: A member of a city council, in NT of the Sanhedrin at Jerusalem.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “member of a council.” It identifies a person who belongs to a council, rather than the council as a group. The word occurs twice in the Greek New Testament, once in Mark and once in Luke. Its basic sense is therefore a council member or participant, while the surrounding verse determines the person’s particular role or situation.

d: The assembly or body of elders.

e.t: This word refers to an assembly or council made up of elders. It names a gathered body of older or recognized leaders rather than an individual elder. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 5:21, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. The phrases “assembly of the elders” and “council of elders” emphasize the same central idea. It is best understood as a collective term for that council or assembly.

d: To separate, distinguish, discern one thing from another; to doubt, hesitate, waver.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word describes judging between possibilities, making a distinction, or discerning what is true; in some settings, it refers to doubting or hesitating. Its central idea is an inward weighing that may lead either to a clear judgment or to uncertainty. It occurs 19 times in 18 New Testament verses, including uses translated “doubt,” “judge,” and “discern.” The surrounding sentence determines whether the emphasis is careful distinction or unsettled doubt.

d: A judge.

e.t: This word means “judge,” referring to a person whose role is to decide a matter or render a judgment. It is used twice in the Greek New Testament, both times in Acts 7. The word identifies judging as an official function rather than merely expressing a personal opinion. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic meaning remains clear: a judge is one who evaluates a case and gives a decision.

d: Hard to understand.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “hard to understand.” It describes something difficult to grasp clearly, whether because the idea is complex or requires careful thought. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, at 2 Peter 3:16. Its basic sense identifies difficulty in understanding rather than declaring that something is impossible to understand; the surrounding passage determines the particular matter being described. d: To write upon, inscribe, imprint a mark on.
me: Verb, Future, Active, Indicative, first, Singular

Verb, pLuperfect, Passive, Indicative, third, Singular

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to write” or “to write on.” It describes putting words, a message, or an inscription into written form, including writing something upon a surface or object. Its central idea is the deliberate recording of words so they can be read or recognized. The word occurs five times in the Greek New Testament, with two occurrences in Hebrews and one each in Mark, Acts, and Revelation.

d: To call; to choose for myself; pass: to be named.
me: Verb, Aorist, Middle, Participle, Nominative, Singular, Masculine
Verb, Present, Passive, Participle, Nominative, Singular, Feminine

e.t: This word expresses being “called” or “chosen,” and can describe the act of calling or choosing someone. It functions as a word about designation—someone being called by a particular name or selected for a purpose. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, in John 5:2 and Acts 15:40. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage, but its central idea remains calling or choosing.

d: Evening.

e.t: This word means “evening,” referring to the later part of the day as daylight fades and night approaches. It identifies a time of day rather than an action, person, or spiritual quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, in Luke and Acts. Its meaning remains straightforward, while the surrounding verse determines what happened during that evening or why that time is mentioned.

d: An evangelist, a missionary, bearer of good tidings.

e.t: The word means “evangelist.” It names a person identified by that title, rather than an object, action, or place. In the Greek New Testament, it appears three times: in Acts 21:8, Ephesians 4:11, and 2 Timothy 4:5. These occurrences show the term being used as a personal designation across different passages. Its precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage, whose text is not included here.

d: Euodia, a Christian woman of Philippi.

e.t: Euodia is the personal name of a person mentioned in the Greek New Testament. It is rendered “Euodia,” and it occurs once, in Philippians 4:2. As a name, it identifies an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general concept. The word itself does not provide a wider definition beyond that personal designation. Its precise role in the verse depends on the surrounding passage, while its lexical contribution remains the person’s name.

d: A cultivated olive tree.

e.t: This word means “cultivated olive tree,” referring to an olive tree grown and cared for rather than a wild one. It can also be expressed simply as “olive tree,” but its fuller sense highlights cultivation. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Romans 11:24, so its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage. Its basic meaning remains a particular kind of olive tree: one associated with deliberate planting, tending, and growth.

d: To mix, mingle, pour out for drinking.

e.t: This Greek New Testament verb means “to mix”: to combine one thing with another so that they form a mixture. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. The word occurs three times in the Greek New Testament, all within Revelation, and is rendered “mix” in its recorded English support. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and comparison being made.

d: Most excellent, an official epithet, used in addressing a Roman of high rank, and in the second century one of equestrian (as distinguished from senatorial) rank.

e.t: This word describes someone or something as “excellent” or “most excellent.” It expresses a high degree of distinction or quality and can function as a respectful description of a person. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs four times, all in Luke and Acts. Its use in formal address shows that it can identify someone viewed as especially distinguished. The exact force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding wording and situation.

d: A charitable gift, public service in the widest sense; service as of priest or Levite ritual.

e.t: This word means “ministry” or “religious service”: work performed for God or for the benefit of others. It can describe priestly service, faithful Christian labor, or practical service that meets the needs of God’s people. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs six times, including passages concerning priestly duties and devoted service in Christian ministry. Its central idea is active service offered as a sacred responsibility rather than merely private belief or intention.

d: To make a disciple of, train in discipleship; pass: to be trained, discipled, instructed.

e.t: This Greek New Testament verb means “to disciple” or “to teach.” It describes helping people become disciples—learners who follow instruction and are formed as followers. Depending on the sentence, it may emphasize the act of making disciples or the teaching involved in that process. The word occurs four times in the Greek New Testament, appearing in Matthew and Acts. Its central idea is not merely passing along information, but bringing people into the role and practice of a disciple.

d: Melchi, one of the ancestors of Jesus.

e.t: Melki is a personal name, rendered as “Melki.” It identifies an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Luke 3, at Luke 3:24 and Luke 3:28. Because the available information does not include the surrounding verse text, its specific genealogical place cannot be explained here; however, its basic lexical function is clear: it is the name Melki.

d: (a) a distributing, a distribution, (b) a parting, dividing, severance, separation.

e.t: The word refers to “dividing” or “division”: separation that distinguishes one thing from another or separates something into parts. It names the idea of division rather than describing a person or object. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Hebrews, so its meaning is focused and consistent rather than broadly varied across many books. The precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, which is not included here.

d: A temple, a shrine, that part of the temple where God himself resides.

e.t: This word means “temple,” referring to a sacred place set apart for worship. It is a noun used for the temple as a recognized holy building or sanctuary, whether speaking about its structure, its courts, or what takes place there. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 45 times, showing that the temple is an important setting in the Gospel accounts and Revelation. Its exact force in any passage depends on the surrounding verse and its use of the word.

d: Yet, nevertheless, even.
me: ADVerb or adverb and particle combined

e.t: This word means “just as.” It is an expression that connects one statement with another by showing that something is true in the same way or under a corresponding comparison. Its basic force is straightforward: it links ideas through likeness or agreement rather than introducing a new subject. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, appearing once each in John, 1 Corinthians, and Galatians. The surrounding sentence determines exactly what two statements are being connected.

d: Woe!, alas!, uttered in grief or denunciation.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “woe!” It is an exclamation that expresses a strong declaration of distress or calamity. Rather than naming a person, object, or action, it functions as an utterance spoken or written to call attention to a grave condition. The word occurs 46 times in the Greek New Testament, showing repeated use in solemn declarations throughout that corpus.

d: Very costly, very precious, of great value.

e.t: This word describes something expensive or valuable—something that carries a high cost or worth. It can describe material possessions or adornment, but its central idea is high value rather than mere beauty or usefulness. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, including descriptions of costly items and valuable qualities. The surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis falls on monetary expense, preciousness, or significant worth.

d: A porch, court before a building, vestibule.

e.t: This word means “entryway,” referring to an entrance area or passage leading into a building or enclosed place. It names a location rather than a person, action, or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Mark 14:68. The word’s basic sense identifies the place itself; the precise significance of that location in the verse depends on the surrounding passage.

d: An offering, sacrifice.

e.t: This word means “offering”: something presented or given. It names what is brought before God or set apart as a gift, sacrifice, or service, depending on the surrounding passage. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs nine times, including five occurrences in Hebrews and others in Acts, Romans, and Ephesians. Its central idea remains the act or object of presenting something, while the specific kind of offering must be understood from the verse and its context.

d: A prophetess.

e.t: “Prophetess” means a woman who speaks or serves in the role associated with a prophet. The word identifies a female prophet without, by itself, explaining the specific message, authority, or faithfulness involved in a particular passage. It appears twice in the Greek New Testament, once in Luke and once in Revelation. Its exact significance in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains a woman recognized as a prophetess.

d: To appoint, choose, elect, take into hand.
me: Verb, Aorist, middle Deponent, Indicative, third, Singular

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “appointed,” “to appoint,” or “to choose.” It describes the act of selecting someone for a particular responsibility, place, or purpose. The word appears three times in the Greek New Testament, all in Acts, so its basic sense is focused and specific rather than broadly distributed. It is used in Acts 3:20, Acts 22:14, and Acts 26:16. The surrounding passage determines exactly who is appointed and what purpose the appointment serves.

d: Rehoboam, son of Solomon, and King of Israel.

e.t: Rehoboam is a personal name referring to a person named in the Greek New Testament. The name appears twice in the Greek New Testament, both times in Matthew 1:7. Its meaning is therefore primarily identifying: it distinguishes this individual from the other people named in the genealogy. The supplied material does not provide a broader definition, description, or verse context, so the safest explanation is simply that Rehoboam is the person’s name, preserved in this Greek New Testament genealogy.

d: Filth, filthiness, dirt, squalor.

e.t: This word means “dirt” or “filth,” referring to something unclean or soiled. It occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in 1 Peter 3:21. These meanings describe the ordinary sense of the word, while the surrounding verse determines how Peter applies it there. The word itself points to uncleanness rather than presenting a broad range of meanings or repeated uses across different passages.

d: Siloam, a spring within the walls, in the south-east corner of Jerusalem.

e.t: Siloam is the name of a specific place in Jerusalem, not a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the New Testament, it is preserved as a place name and appears three times: once in Luke and twice in John. The name is connected with references to the location called Siloam, but the supplied information does not include the surrounding verse text needed to explain what happens in each passage. Its meaning is therefore straightforward: Siloam identifies that particular place.

d: Made of emerald, emerald-green.
me: Adjective, Accusative, Plural, Masculine, NUmerical Indiclinable (A)

e.t: This word means “emerald,” the name of a precious green stone. It names the gemstone itself rather than an action, quality, or person. It occurs once in the Greek New Testament, at Revelation 4:3. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the word’s precise descriptive role in that verse must be understood from its context. Its central meaning remains the gemstone called an emerald.

d: Simeon or Simon.

e.t: Simeon is a personal name, referring to people identified by that name rather than describing a quality, action, or object. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs seven times across seven verses. The name appears in Luke, Acts, 2 Peter, and Revelation, including references to more than one person named Simeon. Its precise significance in any particular passage comes from the surrounding verse and context.

d: A title, inscription.

e.t: This word means a “sign” or “title”—a written designation that identifies someone or states who they are. It can refer to a notice placed where others can read it, or to the title assigned to a person. In the Greek New Testament, it appears twice, both times in John 19. Its precise force in either occurrence is clarified by the surrounding passage, but its central idea is a written identifying designation.

d: Endurance, steadfastness, patient waiting for.

e.t: This word means “perseverance”: steady endurance that continues rather than giving up. It describes a settled quality of remaining faithful and persistent through difficulty, delay, or opposition. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 32 times, showing that perseverance is a recurring part of faithful living, not a rare or isolated idea. Its precise emphasis in a particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central sense remains continued steadfastness. d: Philippi, a great city of the Roman province Macedonia.

e.t: This word is the place-name “Philippi.” It identifies the same named location whenever it appears in the Greek New Testament, rather than describing an action, quality, or person. It occurs four times in four New Testament verses: Acts 16:12, Acts 20:6, Philippians 1:1, and 1 Thessalonians 2:2. Its precise significance in any one passage comes from that passage’s surrounding text, not from the name alone.
